blocks.x: Instrumentation as infrastructure: versioned schemas per device class, store-and-forward capture that survives partitions, heartbeat monitoring that catches zombie devices — wired into brownfield PLCs and protocols that were never meant to interoperate.
Every downstream promise rests on capture fidelity

Sensor fabric is the difference between an IoT program and a box of dashboards: every device class speaks a versioned schema, every gateway survives disconnection, and every device has an owner, a firmware version and an end-of-life date. The unglamorous parts — provisioning, OTA, schema registries — are the program.

The practice covers brownfield retrofit (a factory in 1998 speaks Modbus, and that is fine), greenfield instrumentation, gateway design, and the fleet operations that keep thousands of devices observable and updatable.
Below: the failure modes that corrupt sensor estates, the reference architecture of the fabric, and the console that keeps fidelity honest.
Four failure modes that corrupt sensor estates
Each of these silently poisons everything downstream — analytics, twins and predictions all inherit the rot — which is why the countermeasures live at the capture layer.

blocks.x: Reference architecture — the sensor fabric from field to broker

Device classes carry versioned schemas, gateways buffer through partitions with store-and-forward guarantees, the broker normalizes without losing provenance, and heartbeat monitors treat a silent device as an incident — fidelity is enforced at the layer where it is won or lost.

nodes.label: PLCs & RTUs
nodes.detail: Control-layer devices on isolated field buses; the fabric reads via protocol adapters — never writes without a signed change window.

nodes.label: Historians
nodes.detail: Existing process historians joined as first-class sources — their archives migrate with provenance and unit contracts.

nodes.label: Edge gateways
nodes.detail: Protocol translation (Modbus, OPC-UA, proprietary) with unit normalization and local buffering — gateways hold their line offline.

nodes.label: OT/IT DMZ
nodes.detail: Controlled conduits between zones — brokers with allow-lists, unidirectional paths where the risk profile demands them.

nodes.label: Asset inventory
nodes.detail: Passive-discovery asset inventory with per-device identity — the estate knows what is on its networks, including what was never registered.

nodes.label: Time-series core
nodes.detail: Industrial time-series store with retention tiers and downsampling — the analytics practices read from contracts, not from raw dumps.

nodes.label: Patch planning
nodes.detail: Firmware and PLC patching scheduled against process windows — the shutdown calendar is the patch calendar, by joint agreement with OT.

widgets.note: Click zones for the conduit contract each boundary carries. The read-only default at the PLC boundary is the OT team's non-negotiable — and ours.

widgets.title: Instrumentation what-if — coverage, quality gates, cost
widgets.note: The cost curve argues for instrumenting by priority tier: P1 coverage buys the analytics value; P5 coverage buys the invoice. The quality gates quarantine rather than average — noise stays visible.

blocks.x: Integration surface — PLCs, gateways and the historians

The fabric wraps brownfield reality: PLCs, legacy protocols and historians are the integration scope, and the contracts define what each device class must emit and how brownfield impedance is handled.
Data-integrity governance overlay
Provenance survives the pipeline: every reading carries device identity, schema version and gateway path — so a suspect reading can be traced to hardware, firmware or transport in one query.

items: Unversioned payloads quarantine at the edge
Alarm paths never compete with bulk
Every device has an owner and an end-of-life

blocks.x: Zombie sweeps run monthly: devices that heartbeat but emit flat-lined or physically implausible values are flagged for field verification — silent failure is the fabric's most expensive failure mode.
